usage: Telling someone to enter, or saying you are entering. Said to a guest at the door.
Polite invitation to enter a room or house.
examples: 들어와요 to a friend at the door.
What time do you come home?
들어오다 often means 'come home' in daily talk.
방 (room) + 에 marks where you enter.
nuance: 들어오다 is 'to come in' — entering toward where the speaker is. Use 들어가다 instead when someone enters moving away from you. In everyday life 들어오다 very often means 'to come home' (집에 들어오다).
mistakes: Saying 들어가요 when you mean entering toward yourself — use 들어와요 for 'come in (here)'.

usage: Can also mean facing a direction.
examples: -고 있어요 = in the middle of doing.
nuance: 향하다 means to head or face toward a direction or destination, which is marked with 으로/로. It sounds a little more formal than 가다, so in casual speech people often just say 가다. It can also mean 'to face' (a direction).
mistakes: Marking the destination with 에 — 향하다 takes 으로/로: '집으로 향해요', not '집에 향해요'.

usage: 머물다 = to stay somewhere for a time.
examples: I'm staying in Seoul for a few days.
I stayed at my friend's place.
I want to stay here longer.
nuance: 머물다 is a ㄹ-stem verb: the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ (머뭅니다, 머무세요), and the 어 form is 머물러요. It means staying somewhere temporarily, like a hotel or a friend's house. In casual travel talk 있다 ('be/stay') is also common: '호텔에 있어요'.
mistakes: Writing the formal form as 머물습니다 — the ㄹ drops, so it is 머뭅니다.
Forgetting the 어 form is 머물러요, not 머물어요.

usage: 다가오다 = move closer toward the speaker.
Also used for time/events getting near.
examples: The dog came up to me.
nuance: 다가오다 means coming nearer toward the speaker — a person, animal, or even time approaching. The opposite direction (moving closer away from you) is 다가가다. For events and dates, it nicely captures 'is approaching'.
mistakes: Mixing up direction: use 다가오다 for coming toward you, 다가가다 for going toward something else.

usage: 다가가다 = move closer toward something/someone else.
Used when you move toward a target away from the speaker.
examples: I go closer to the window.
nuance: 다가가다 is the 'going' counterpart of 다가오다: you move closer toward a target that is away from the speaker. Think 가다 (go) plus 'closer'. For something approaching toward you, switch to 다가오다.
mistakes: Using 다가가다 when something moves toward you — that is 다가오다.

usage: Said when leaving home; literally 'I'll go and come back'.
Take care / See you (when someone leaves)
examples: I'll go to the restroom (and come back).
Polite way to step away briefly.
잘 다녀오다 = to go and return safely.
nuance: 다녀오다 packs 'go AND come back' into one verb, so it's the natural thing to say when you leave but will return. 다녀올게요 (I'm off) and 다녀오세요 (take care / see you) are everyday home phrases. If you are leaving for good, use 가다 instead.
mistakes: Saying just 가요 when leaving home — Koreans say 다녀올게요 to signal you'll be back.

usage: 들어서다 = cross into a place, often the moment of entering.
Emphasizes the act of entering a space.
examples: I opened the door and stepped inside.
When I stepped into the room, it was warm.
nuance: 들어서다 highlights the moment of crossing into a place — stepping over the threshold — while 들어가다/들어오다 focus on the direction of entering. For a total beginner, 들어가다 (go in) and 들어오다 (come in) are more common; 들어서다 adds the nuance of 'just setting foot inside'.
mistakes: Treating 들어서다 as identical to 들어가다 — 들어서다 stresses the act of stepping in, not the direction.

english: to go over / to pass over
usage: Let's go over to the next page
넘어가다 = move across/over to the next thing.
examples: Let's move on to the next question.
Very common in class or meetings.
The sun went down behind the mountain.
Also used for the sun setting.
nuance: 넘어가다 literally means going over something (a hill, a wall) to the other side, and figuratively 'moving on' to the next page, topic, or step. It's everywhere in lessons and meetings: '다음으로 넘어가요' (let's move on). The destination/next item takes 으로/로.
mistakes: Confusing 넘어가다 (go over to the other side) with 넘어지다 (to fall down) — different verbs.

usage: 돌다 = change direction or spin around.
examples: I went around the park once.
The top spins round and round.
nuance: 돌다 is a ㄹ-stem verb meaning to turn, spin, or go around. The ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ, giving 돕니다 (formal) and 도세요 ('please turn' for directions). For turning something else (like a handle), use the related verb 돌리다.
mistakes: Writing the polite request as 돌으세요 — the ㄹ drops, so it is 도세요.
Saying 돕니다 wrong as 돌습니다; the ㄹ-stem rule removes the ㄹ.

usage: 돌리다 = turn an object or body part (something gets turned).
examples: I turned my head to the left.
I ran the washing machine today.
nuance: 돌리다 is the transitive partner of 돌다: you turn something (a handle, your head) or 'run' a machine like a washer. It is a regular 이-stem verb, so the 어 form is 돌려요. If the thing turns by itself, use 돌다 instead.
mistakes: Mixing up 돌다 (turn by itself) and 돌리다 (turn something) — the washing machine is 돌려요 because you operate it.

english: to set out / to step forward
usage: 나서다 = head out, start a journey.
examples: I set out from home early in the morning.
집을 나서다 = leave home / set out.
I set off on a trip.
nuance: 나서다 means to set out or head off (집을 나서다 = leave home to start your day) and also to step forward physically. It carries a sense of starting to move out into the open. For simply 'leaving' a place, 나가다 is the more basic choice.
mistakes: Confusing 나서다 (set out / step forward) with 나가다 (go out) — 나서다 often implies beginning a journey.

english: to run into / to bump into
usage: 마주치다 = meet by chance; the person takes 를/을.
examples: I ran into a friend on the street.
I happened to run into my teacher.
nuance: 마주치다 means to run into someone or something unexpectedly, often by chance. The person you meet takes 를/을 (친구를 마주치다), and it's also the set phrase for eye contact: 눈이 마주치다. For a planned meeting use 만나다 instead.
mistakes: Using 마주치다 for a planned meet-up — that is 만나다. 마주치다 is by chance.
